Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma is of- ten a late complication of AIDS,1 and its incidence in HIV- infected individuals is about 60 times greater than in the general population.1-3 Histologically, it is usually diffuse large cell lymphoma (see Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphomas, above) or small non-cleaved lymphoma (Burkitt’s lym- phoma—see below).1,2,4 About 50% of these are associat- ed with the presence of Epstein-Barr virus. The other com- mon HIV-associated lymphoma is primary CNS lymphoma, which is invariably associated with Epstein- Barr virus.1,4 More recently, primary effusion lymphoma or body cavity-based lymphoma has been identified,1,2,4 which is associated with human herpes virus 8. Although Hodgkin’s disease (see above) is not considered an AIDS- defining illness, epidemiological studies have shown it to be associated with HIV infection.5 The introduction of HAART for HIV infection (p.856) may reduce the risk of lymphomas by improving immune function,2,4,6 but, con- versely, may increase the incidence by allowing patients to survive long enough for lymphoma to develop.1,2 The in- cidence of primary CNS lymphoma has decreased with the advent of HAART.1,6 There is some evidence of tumour response when antiretroviral therapy is started in a patient who already has a lymphoma.4 A few patients with AIDS-related non-Hodgkin’s lympho- mas present with localised disease, and may benefit from radiotherapy, but most have disseminated disease, often extranodal, at presentation.1,2,4 Optimal management is not established.7 The common chemotherapy
